explanation: Step 1: PCIe x16 slots feature a plastic retention clip at the rear to lock heavy GPUs in place during transport. Step 2: Keys (plastic blocks inside the slot) map to notches on the card edge, physically blocking incorrect voltage/standard cards. Step 3: The 'x16' designation directly dictates the long physical length of the slot for 16 data lanes.
trick: Trap: Forgetting to push the retention clip before removing a GPU will rip the slot off the motherboard.
tip: Keys prevent bad insertions. Retention clips hold heavy GPUs safely.

question: Consider the following statements comparing parallel and serial internal connections: Statement I: PATA (IDE) cables suffered heavily from cross-talk (electromagnetic interference) at high speeds because multiple wires transmitted simultaneously. Statement II: SATA cables solved cross-talk by transmitting data one bit at a time, allowing for much higher clock frequencies. Which is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Parallel ATA (IDE) used 40 or 80 wires. As speeds increased, the signals on adjacent wires interfered with each other (cross-talk), creating a hard speed ceiling. Step 2: Serial ATA (SATA) transmits one bit sequentially. With no adjacent data wires to cause interference, engineers could crank the clock speed up massively, making serial ironically much faster than parallel.
trick: Trap: Intuitively, sending 8 bits at once should be faster. In reality, physics limits parallel bus speeds, making serial the modern winner.
tip: Serial interfaces beat parallel because they eliminate wire-to-wire cross-talk.

question: Match the legacy motherboard form factors to their historical significance: List I (A. AT, B. Baby AT, C. ATX) with List II (1. Standardized in 1995 by Intel, placing I/O ports directly on the board edge, 2. The massive original 1984 IBM format that dominated early PCs, 3. A condensed version of the IBM format that fit in smaller desktop cases).
explanation: Step 1: The AT (Advanced Technology) was IBM's massive original standard. Step 2: Baby AT was a smaller, widely cloned variant that ruled the early 90s. Both lacked integrated I/O blocks (ports required ribbon cables to the case). Step 3: ATX (Advanced Technology eXtended) revolutionized design by integrating the block of I/O ports (USB, audio) directly onto the rear edge of the board.
trick: Trap: Not realizing ATX was the turning point for integrated I/O shields on the back of the PC.
tip: ATX (1995) introduced the modern integrated rear I/O port layout.

question: Consider the following statements regarding BIOS interface paradigms: Statement I: Traditional BIOS can only be navigated using a keyboard because it lacks mouse drivers and graphical support. Statement II: UEFI interfaces often include full graphical user interfaces (GUIs), mouse support, and internet connectivity. Which is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: The legacy BIOS environment operates in 16-bit real mode. It is entirely text-based (usually blue and white) and relies purely on keyboard arrow keys for navigation. Step 2: UEFI operates in 32-bit or 64-bit mode, supporting high-resolution graphics, mouse input, and even basic networking to download updates directly from within the firmware interface.
trick: Trap: Assuming you could always use a mouse in BIOS. Mice strictly require OS-level or UEFI-level drivers.
tip: Legacy BIOS = Keyboard/Text only. UEFI = Mouse/GUI support.

question: Match the legacy video interfaces with their cable configurations: List I (A. Composite Video, B. S-Video, C. Component Video) with List II (1. A single yellow RCA cable carrying all video data, 2. Three RCA cables (Red, Green, Blue) splitting color data for high definition, 3. A round 4-pin connector splitting brightness and color).
explanation: Step 1: Composite video squashes all luma (brightness) and chroma (color) into one low-quality yellow RCA cable. Step 2: S-Video (Separate Video) improves quality by separating luma and chroma into different pins in a round DIN connector. Step 3: Component Video splits the signal into three distinct RCA cables (YPbPr) for HD analog transmission.
trick: Trap: Confusing Composite and Component. Composite 'composes' it all into one yellow wire. Component breaks it down into parts (RGB).
tip: Composite = 1 Yellow cable. Component = 3 RGB cables.

question: Consider the following statements regarding expansion bus architectures: Statement I: Standard PCI devices share a common bus, meaning if three cards transmit simultaneously, the total bandwidth is divided among them. Statement II: PCIe devices each have dedicated lanes to the PCIe controller or CPU, guaranteeing unshared bandwidth. Which is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Legacy PCI is a 'multi-drop' shared bus. All devices talk on the same wire, causing traffic jams (like a busy single-lane road). Statement I is true. Step 2: PCIe uses point-to-point switching. A dedicated set of lanes connects each slot to the CPU/Chipset, ensuring full speed for every device without sharing. Statement II is true.
trick: Trap: Understanding why PCIe replaced PCI. Dedicated lanes eliminate bandwidth sharing bottlenecks.
tip: PCI = Shared bandwidth bus. PCIe = Dedicated unshared lanes.

question: Match the Ethernet standards with their naming conventions and speeds: List I (A. 10Base-T, B. 100Base-TX, C. 1000Base-T) with List II (1. Gigabit Ethernet, 2. Fast Ethernet, 3. Standard Legacy Ethernet).
explanation: Step 1: 10Base-T operates at 10 Mbps and is simply referred to as standard Ethernet. Step 2: 100Base-TX operates at 100 Mbps and was branded 'Fast Ethernet' in the late 90s. Step 3: 1000Base-T operates at 1000 Mbps (1 Gbps) and is universally known as Gigabit Ethernet.
trick: Trap: Confusing Fast Ethernet and Gigabit. 'Fast' sounds impressive but is only 100 Mbps, ten times slower than modern Gigabit standards.
tip: 10 = Ethernet. 100 = Fast Ethernet. 1000 = Gigabit Ethernet.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the modern M.2 expansion slot: Statement I: All M.2 slots exclusively support NVMe (PCIe) solid-state drives. Statement II: M.2 slots can be 'keyed' differently (like B key or M key) to restrict insertion to compatible SATA or PCIe modules. Which is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: M.2 is just a physical form factor. Some M.2 slots are wired for standard SATA (slow), some for NVMe/PCIe (fast), and some for both. Statement I is false. Step 2: To prevent inserting an NVMe drive into a SATA-only slot, M.2 drives and slots use physical notches called 'Keys' (B, M, or B+M). Statement II is true.
trick: Trap: Assuming M.2 always implies high NVMe speeds. An M.2 SATA drive is exactly as slow as a traditional 2.5-inch SSD.
tip: M.2 is a shape. It can carry slow SATA or fast NVMe protocols.

question: Match the following common BIOS/UEFI settings with their functional outcomes: List I (A. XMP/EXPO, B. Boot Sequence, C. Virtualization Technology/VT-x) with List II (1. Determines whether the PC looks at the USB or Hard Drive first to load an OS, 2. Allows running software like VirtualBox or VMware efficiently, 3. Loads an overclocking profile to run RAM at advertised high speeds).
explanation: Step 1: XMP (Intel) or EXPO (AMD) are profiles enabled in BIOS to force RAM to run at its rated high speed rather than the slow default JEDEC standard. Step 2: Boot Sequence/Priority tells the motherboard exactly which drive contains the operating system. Step 3: Hardware Virtualization (VT-x or AMD-V) must be enabled in BIOS to run Virtual Machines.
trick: Trap: Forgetting to enable XMP. If you buy 3600MHz RAM and don't enable XMP in BIOS, it will run at a slow baseline like 2133MHz.
tip: Enable XMP in BIOS to get the RAM speed you paid for.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the RJ-45 connector: Statement I: 'RJ' stands for Registered Jack, and it uses an 8P8C (8 Position, 8 Contact) wiring layout. Statement II: The connector physically restricts the cable to unidirectional transmission (download only). Which is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: RJ-45 is part of the standardized telecom Registered Jack system, using 8 physical slots (Positions) with 8 metal pins (Contacts) inside. Statement I is true. Step 2: Ethernet cables using RJ-45 contain 4 pairs of wires, allowing full-duplex transmission (simultaneous upload and download). Statement II is false.
trick: Trap: Thinking Ethernet is purely one-way. It is full-duplex, meaning traffic flows both ways at the same time.
tip: RJ-45 (8P8C) supports full-duplex, bi-directional Ethernet traffic.
